narrative:
The model estimates a 46% chance that you will leave your job, which is high enough for the company to deny your promotion as a precaution.

Three main factors shaped this outlook. First, your total years of experience across all jobs had the strongest influence and pulled the prediction toward staying. At 1-5 years you are in the most common group among employees expected to remain, yet the model still saw this shorter track record as a reason for caution. Second, having received other job offers while at the company was the strongest factor pushing toward leaving. This signal of external opportunities raised the likelihood you might depart. Third, working in the “other” sector also nudged the prediction upward. While this sector represents about 22% of employees predicted to stay, it appears linked to higher turnover in the model’s view.

Taken together, your solid emotional commitment, satisfaction with rewards, and convenient commute worked in your favor, but they were not enough to outweigh the combination of limited overall experience, outside offers, and sector patterns.

The organization should discuss retention steps with you, such as faster promotion paths, targeted training, or clearer career growth. You may want to reflect on whether those external opportunities better match your goals. Addressing these points openly could change the outlook for both sides.
